claim: Bioimage analysis of fluorescent labels is widely used in the life sciences.
source: Bioimage analysis of fluorescent labels is widely used in the life sciences.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field presented in the abstract without specific data or citations in this sentence.

claim: Recent advances in deep learning allow automating time-consuming manual image analysis processes based on annotated training data.
source: Recent advances in deep learning (DL) allow automating time-consuming manual image analysis processes based on annotated training data.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge in the field of deep learning applications.

claim: Manual annotation of fluorescent features with a low signal-to-noise ratio is somewhat subjective.
source: However, manual annotation of fluorescent features with a low signal-to-noise ratio is somewhat subjective.
evidence: This is a claim about the nature of manual annotation that is supported by citations later in the manuscript.

claim: Training DL models on subjective annotations may be unstable or yield biased models.
source: Training DL models on subjective annotations may be instable or yield biased models.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential consequences of using subjective annotations.

claim: Ground truth estimation from multiple human annotators helps to establish objectivity in fluorescent feature annotations.
source: With data from two model organisms (mice, zebrafish) and five laboratories, we show that ground truth estimation from multiple human annotators helps to establish objectivity in fluorescent feature annotations.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from multiple datasets.

claim: Ensembles of multiple models trained on the estimated ground truth establish reliability and validity.
source: Furthermore, ensembles of multiple models trained on the estimated ground truth establish reliability and validity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Fluorescence does not provide clear signal-to-noise borders.
source: However, fluorescence does not provide clear signal-to-noise borders, forcing human experts to utilize individual heuristic criteria, such as morphology, size, or signal intensity to classify fluorescent signals as background, or to, often manually, annotate them as a region of interest (ROI).
evidence: This is a statement about the inherent properties of fluorescence imaging.

claim: Human experts utilize individual heuristic criteria such as morphology, size, or signal intensity to classify fluorescent signals.
source: However, fluorescence does not provide clear signal-to-noise borders, forcing human experts to utilize individual heuristic criteria, such as morphology, size, or signal intensity to classify fluorescent signals as background, or to, often manually, annotate them as a region of interest (ROI).
evidence: This describes the manual annotation process used by experts.

claim: The cognitive decision process in fluorescent feature annotation depends on the graphical perception capabilities of the individual annotator.
source: This cognitive decision process depends on the graphical perception capabilities of the individual annotator (Cleveland and McGill, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cleveland and McGill, 1985.

claim: Constant technological advances in fluorescence microscopy facilitate the automatized acquisition of large image datasets.
source: Constant technological advances in fluorescence microscopy facilitate the automatized acquisition of large image datasets, even at high resolution and with high throughput (Li et al., 2010; McDole et al., 2018; Osten and Margrie, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Traditional image thresholding techniques frequently lack flexibility as they rely on a high signal-to-noise ratio or require computational expertise.
source: However, attempts to replace human experts and to automate the annotation process using traditional image thresholding techniques (e.g. histogram shape-, entropy-, or clustering-based methods [Sezgin and Sankur, 2004]) frequently lack flexibility, as they rely on a high signal-to-noise ratio in the images or require computational expertise for user-based adaptation to individual datasets (von Chamier et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sezgin and Sankur, 2004 and von Chamier et al., 2019.

claim: Deep convolutional neural networks have shown remarkable capacities in image recognition tasks.
source: In recent years, deep learning (DL) and in particular deep convolutional neural networks have shown remarkable capacities in image recognition tasks, opening new possibilities to perform automatized image analysis.
evidence: This is a general statement about the capabilities of deep learning supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: DL-based approaches have emerged as an alternative to conventional feature annotation or segmentation methods.
source: DL-based approaches have emerged as an alternative to conventional feature annotation or segmentation methods (Caicedo et al., 2019) and are even capable of performing complex tasks such as artificial labeling of plain bright-field images (von Chamier et al., 2019; Christiansen et al., 2018; Ounkomol et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The main difference between conventional and DL algorithms is that conventional algorithms follow predefined rules while DL algorithms are flexible to learn the respective task based on a training dataset.
source: The main difference between conventional and DL algorithms is that conventional algorithms follow predefined rules (hard-coded), while DL algorithms are flexible to learn the respective task on base of a training dataset (LeCun et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to LeCun et al., 2015.

claim: Deployment of DL approaches necessitates both computational expertise and suitable computing resources.
source: Yet, deployment of DL approaches necessitates both computational expertise and suitable computing resources.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical requirements for using DL.

claim: Initial efforts have been made to break down barriers to DL deployment by integration into prevalent bioimaging tools such as ImageJ and CellProfiler, or using cloud-based approaches.
source: Initial efforts have already been made to break down these barriers, for instance, by integration into prevalent bioimaging tools such as ImageJ (Falk et al., 2019) and CellProfiler (McQuin et al., 2018), or using cloud-based approaches (Haberl et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific tools and approaches.

claim: DL-based methods require integration into the bioimage analysis pipeline to harness their potentials.
source: To harness the potentials of these DL-based methods, they require integration into the bioimage analysis pipeline.
evidence: This is an inference about what is needed for effective use of DL methods.

claim: DL-based approaches must meet the same standards as any method in an empirical study: objectivity, reliability, and validity.
source: We argue that such an integration into the scientific process ultimately necessitates DL-based approaches to meet the same standards as any method in an empirical study. We can derive these standards from the general quality criteria of qualitative and quantitative research: objectivity, reliability, and validity (Frambach et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Frambach et al., 2013 regarding research quality criteria.

claim: Manual annotation of fluorescent features has long been known to be subjective, especially in the case of weak signal-to-noise thresholds.
source: Manual annotation of fluorescent features has long been known to be subjective, especially in the case of weak signal-to-noise thresholds (Schmitz et al., 1999; Collier et al., 2003; Niedworok et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: There is no objective ground truth reference in the particular case of fluorescent label segmentation.
source: Notably, there is no objective ground truth reference in the particular case of fluorescent label segmentation, causing a critical problem for training and evaluation of DL algorithms.
evidence: This is a statement about a fundamental challenge in fluorescent label segmentation.

claim: Annotations of low quality can cause DL algorithms to either fail to train or to reproduce inconsistent annotations on new data.
source: As multiple studies have pointed out that annotations of low quality can cause DL algorithms to either fail to train or to reproduce inconsistent annotations on new data (von Chamier et al., 2019; Falk et al., 2019), this is a crucial obstacle for applying DL to bioimage analysis processes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to von Chamier et al., 2019 and Falk et al., 2019.

claim: Repeatability or test-retest reliability is guaranteed for any deterministic DL model.
source: Repeatability or test-retest reliability is defined as 'closeness of the agreement between the results of successive measurements of the same measure and carried out under the same conditions' (Taylor and Kuyatt, 1994, 14), which is guaranteed for any deterministic DL model.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Taylor and Kuyatt, 1994 and logical inference about deterministic models.

claim: The output of different DL models trained on the same training dataset can vary significantly due to the stochastic training procedure.
source: This is a critical point, since the output of different DL models trained on the same training dataset can vary significantly. This is caused by the stochastic training procedure (e.g. random initialization, random sampling and data augmentation [Ronneberger et al., 2015]), the choice of model parameters (e.g. model architecture, weights, activation functions), and the choice of hyperparameters (e.g. learning rate, mini-batch size, training epochs).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ronneberger et al., 2015 and describes known properties of DL training.

claim: Validity is typically measured using appropriate similarity measures such as F1 score for detection and Intersection over Union (IoU) for segmentation purposes.
source: On a basis of a given ground truth, validity is typically measured using appropriate similarity measures such as F1 score for detection and Intersection over Union (IoU) for segmentation purposes (Ronneberger et al., 2015; Falk et al., 2019; Caicedo et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple sources describing standard evaluation metrics.

claim: The DL community has established widely accepted standards for training models including techniques to avoid overfitting, tuning hyperparameters, and selecting appropriate metrics for model evaluation.
source: In addition, the DL community has established widely accepted standards for training models. These comprise, among other things, techniques to avoid overfitting (regularization techniques and cross-validation), tuning hyperparameters, and selecting appropriate metrics for model evaluation.
evidence: This describes established practices in the DL community.

claim: These standards do not apply for the training and evaluation of a DL model in the absence of a ground truth, like in the case of fluorescent features.
source: However, these standards do not apply for the training and evaluation of a DL model in the absence of a ground truth, like in the case of fluorescent features.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of standard DL practices in the specific context of fluorescent feature analysis.

claim: There is a reproducibility crisis in the fields of biology, medicine and artificial intelligence.
source: Taken together and with regard to the discussion about a reproducibility crisis in the fields of biology, medicine and artificial intelligence (Siebert et al., 2015; Baker, 2016; Ioannidis, 2016; Hutson, 2018; Fanelli, 2018; Chen et al., 2019), these limitations indicate that DL could aggravate this crisis by adding even more unknowns and uncertainties to bioimage analyses.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to literature discussing the reproducibility crisis.

claim: DL could aggravate the reproducibility crisis by adding more unknowns and uncertainties to bioimage analyses.
source: Taken together and with regard to the discussion about a reproducibility crisis in the fields of biology, medicine and artificial intelligence (Siebert et al., 2015; Baker, 2016; Ioannidis, 2016; Hutson, 2018; Fanelli, 2018; Chen et al., 2019), these limitations indicate that DL could aggravate this crisis by adding even more unknowns and uncertainties to bioimage analyses.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential negative impacts of DL, based on inference from the cited reproducibility crisis literature.

claim: Training of DL models on the pooled input of multiple human experts utilizing ground truth estimation (consensus models) increases objectivity of fluorescent feature segmentation.
source: We show that training of DL models on the pooled input of multiple human experts utilizing ground truth estimation (consensus models) increases objectivity of fluorescent feature segmentation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Ensembles of consensus models are capable of enhancing the reliability and validity of bioimage analysis of ambiguous image data.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that ensembles of consensus models are even capable of enhancing the reliability and validity of bioimage analysis of ambiguous image data, such as fluorescence features in histological tissue sections.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: U-Net and its variants have emerged as the de facto standard for biomedical image segmentation purposes.
source: U-Net and its variants have emerged as the de facto standard for biomedical image segmentation purposes (McQuin et al., 2018; Falk et al., 2019; Caicedo et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple sources.

claim: STAPLE is used to estimate a ground truth and create consensus annotations.
source: Contrary to the first strategy, simultaneous truth and performance level estimation (STAPLE) (Warfield et al., 2004) is used to estimate a ground truth and create consensus annotations.
evidence: This describes a method used in the study, supported by a citation to Warfield et al., 2004.

claim: Model ensembles are known to be more robust to noise.
source: Such model ensembles are known to be more robust to noise (Dietterich, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dietterich, 2000.

claim: Deep ensembles are supposed to yield high-quality predictive uncertainty estimates.
source: Moreover, deep ensembles are supposed to yield high-quality predictive uncertainty estimates (Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017.

claim: cFOS is an activity-dependent transcription factor and its expression in the brain can be modified experimentally by behavioral testing of the animals.
source: cFOS is an activity-dependent transcription factor and its expression in the brain can be modified experimentally by behavioral testing of the animals (Gallo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gallo et al., 2018.

claim: The low signal-to-noise ratio of cFOS, its broad usage in neurobiology and the well-established correlation of its abundance with behavioral paradigms render it an ideal bioimage dataset to test the hypotheses.
source: The low signal-to-noise ratio of this label, its broad usage in neurobiology and the well-established correlation of its abundance with behavioral paradigms render it an ideal bioimage dataset to test our hypotheses (Shuvaev et al., 2017; Gallo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Shuvaev et al., 2017 and Gallo et al., 2018.

claim: A training dataset of 36 images and a test set of nine microscopy images showing cFOS immunoreactivity were manually annotated by five independent experts.
source: To assess the three different strategies, a training dataset of 36 images and a test set of nine microscopy images (1024 × 1024 px, 1.61 px/µm, on average ∼35 nuclei per image, see also Figure 1—figure supplement 2) showing cFOS immunoreactivity were manually annotated by five independent experts (experts 1–5).
evidence: This describes the experimental data collection process.

claim: The analysis revealed substantial differences between the annotations of the different experts and shows varying inter-rater agreement.
source: The analysis revealed substantial differences between the annotations of the different experts and shows varying inter-rater agreement (Schmitz et al., 1999; Collier et al., 2003; Niedworok et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with supporting citations.

claim: The level of inter-rater variability was inversely correlated with the relative signal intensities.
source: The level of inter-rater variability was inversely correlated with the relative signal intensities (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Niedworok et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, supported by a figure and a citation.

claim: Expert models are able to learn and reproduce the annotation behavior of the individual experts.
source: As pointed out by von Chamier et al., 2019, this indicates that our expert models are able to learn and reproduce the annotation behavior of the individual experts.
evidence: This is an inference from the data, supported by a citation to von Chamier et al., 2019.

claim: Expert models yield a lower similarity to the est. GT compared to the consensus models or consensus ensembles.
source: Overall, the expert models yield a lower similarity to the est. GT compared to the consensus models (blue) or consensus ensembles (orange).
evidence: This is a finding from the similarity analysis.

claim: Both consensus models and consensus ensembles perform on par with human experts.
source: Notably, both consensus models and consensus ensembles perform on par with human experts.
evidence: This is a finding from the similarity analysis.

claim: Consensus ensembles outperform all other strategies, even at varying IoU thresholds.
source: Hereby, the consensus ensembles outperform all other strategies, even at varying IoU thresholds (Figure 2F and Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a finding from the similarity analysis, supported by figures.

claim: Consensus ensemble annotations show a high reliability of agreement.
source: Calculating the Fleiss' kappa value (Fleiss and Cohen, 1973) revealed that consensus ensemble annotations show a high reliability of agreement (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is a finding from the reliability analysis, supported by a figure and citation.

claim: The Fleiss' kappa values for consensus ensembles indicate a substantial or almost perfect agreement.
source: Following the Fleiss' kappa interpretation from Landis and Koch, 1977, the results for the consensus ensembles indicate a substantial or almost perfect agreement.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Fleiss' kappa results, supported by a citation to Landis and Koch, 1977.

claim: The Fleiss' kappa values for human experts refer to a fair agreement.
source: In contrast, the Fleiss' kappa values for human experts refer to a fair agreement while the results for the alternative DL strategies lead to a moderate agreement (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is a finding from the reliability analysis, supported by a figure.

claim: Training of DL models solely on the input of a single human expert imposes a high risk of incorporating an intrinsic bias.
source: Starting from the expert model strategy, we seek to establish objectivity (consensus models) and, successively, reliability and validity in the consensus ensemble strategy. In the following analysis, we first turn toward a comprehensive evaluation of the objectivity and its relation to validity before moving on to the concept of reliability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the similarity analysis.

claim: Only the consensus ensemble strategy meets the bioimaging standards for objectivity, reliability, and validity in terms of similarity metrics.
source: We conclude that, in terms of similarity metrics, only the consensus ensemble strategy meet the bioimaging standards for objectivity, reliability, and validity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comprehensive similarity analysis.

claim: Rodents show changes in the distribution and abundance of cFOS in the hippocampus after processing information about places and contexts.
source: It is well established in the neuroscientific literature that rodents show changes in the distribution and abundance of cFOS in a specific brain region, namely the hippocampus, after processing information about places and contexts (Keiser et al., 2017; Campeau et al., 1997; Huff et al., 2006; Ramamoorthi et al., 2011; Tayler et al., 2013; Murawski et al., 2012; Guzowski et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to neuroscience literature.

claim: Fear conditioned mice (C+) showed increased freezing behavior after fear acquisition and showed strong freezing responses when re-exposed to the training context 24 hr later.
source: For instance, fear (threat; LeDoux, 2014) conditioned mice (C+) showed increased freezing behavior after fear acquisition and showed strong freezing responses when re-exposed to the training context 24 hr later (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from the study, supported by a figure.

claim: All models and ensembles show a highly significant context-dependent increase in the number of cFOS-positive nuclei.
source: As indicated before, all models and ensembles show a highly significant context-dependent increase in the number of cFOS-positive nuclei, but also a notable variation in effect sizes for both expert and consensus models.
evidence: This is a finding from the bioimage analysis.

claim: All consensus models and ensembles identify a significant context-dependent increase in the mean signal intensity of cFOS-positive nuclei.
source: Moreover, we identify a significant context-dependent increase in the mean signal intensity of cFOS-positive nuclei for all consensus models and ensembles.
evidence: This is a finding from the bioimage analysis.

claim: All four expert models trained on the annotations of expert 1 did not yield a significant increase in mean signal intensity of cFOS-positive nuclei.
source: The expert models, by contrast, yield a high variation in effect sizes at different significance levels. Interestingly, all four expert models trained on the annotations of expert 1 (and two other expert models only in the case of H vs. C+) did not yield a significant increase, indicating that expert 1's annotation behavior was incorporated into the expert-1-specific models and that this also affects the bioimage analysis results (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from the bioimage analysis, supported by a figure.

claim: The meta analysis discloses a context-dependent increase of cFOS in almost all analyzed hippocampal regions except for the infrapyramidal blade of the dentate gyrus.
source: The meta analysis discloses a context-dependent increase of cFOS in almost all analyzed hippocampal regions (Figure 4A–D), except for the infrapyramidal blade of the dentate gyrus (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analysis, supported by figures.

claim: The majority votes of all three strategies at a significance level of p ≤ 0.05 are identical for each pairwise comparison.
source: Notably, the majority votes of all three strategies at a significance level of p ≤ 0.05 (after Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons) are identical for each pairwise comparison (Figure 4A–E).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis, supported by figures.

claim: Consensus ensembles yield a significantly lower standard deviation of reported effect sizes compared to both alternative strategies.
source: This confirmed the visual impression from Figure 4A–E as the consensus ensembles yield a significantly lower standard deviation compared to both alternative strategies (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a finding from the variation analysis, supported by a figure.

claim: No expert model detected all biological effects in the microscopy images that were defined by the majority votes of all models.
source: This analysis shows that no expert model detected all biological effects in the microscopy images that were defined by the majority votes of all models.
evidence: This is a finding from the variation per model analysis.

claim: The consensus ensemble strategy is best suited to satisfy the bioimaging standards for objectivity, reliability, and validity.
source: Consequently, we conclude that the consensus ensemble strategy is best suited to satisfy the bioimaging standards for objectivity, reliability, and validity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comprehensive bioimage analysis results.

claim: Transfer learning is a technique that enables DL models to reuse the image feature representations learned on another source.
source: Transfer learning is a technique that enables DL models to reuse the image feature representations learned on another source, such as a task (e.g. image segmentation) or a domain (e.g. the fluorescent feature, here cFOS-positive nuclei).
evidence: This describes a known technique in deep learning.

claim: Transfer learning is particularly advantageous when applied to a task or domain where limited training data is available.
source: This is particularly advantageous when applied to a task or domain where limited training data is available (Yosinski et al., 2014; Oquab et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Yosinski et al., 2014 and Oquab et al., 2014.

claim: Transfer learning might be used to reduce observer variability and to increase feature annotation objectivity.
source: Moreover, transfer learning might be used to reduce observer variability and to increase feature annotation objectivity (Bayramoglu and Heikkilä, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bayramoglu and Heikkilä, 2016.

claim: Both from scratch and fine-tuned initiation variants resulted in individual consensus models that reached human expert level performance.
source: Both from scratch and fine-tuned initiation variants resulted in individual consensus models that reached human expert level performance (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the external dataset analysis, supported by figures.

claim: Models adapted from pretrained weights yielded a higher validity in terms of similarity to the estimated ground truth.
source: However, models adapted from pretrained weights yielded a higher validity in terms of similarity to the estimated ground truth.
evidence: This is a finding from the external dataset analysis.

claim: The out-of-the-box segmentation performance of the frozen Lab-Wue1 models was very poor on dissimilar images.
source: Consequently, the out-of-the-box segmentation performance of the frozen Lab-Wue1 models was very poor on dissimilar images (Figure 5D - Lab-Wue2), but we found it to be on par with human experts and adapted models on images that are highly similar to the original dataset (Figure 5D - Lab-Mue - very similar domain and the same task).
evidence: This is a finding from the frozen model analysis, supported by figures.

claim: The bioimage analyses of all DL-based approaches for Lab-Mue revealed a significantly higher number of cFOS-positive cells in the PVT of mice 24 hr after fear conditioning.
source: For Lab-Mue, the bioimage analyses of all DL-based approaches, including the frozen consensus models and ensembles pretrained on Lab-Wue1, revealed a significantly higher number of cFOS-positive cells in the PVT of mice 24 hr after fear conditioning (lRET), which was confirmed by the manual expert analysis (Figure 5E - Lab-Mue, Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the Lab-Mue bioimage analysis, supported by a figure and table.

claim: The formation of model ensembles increased the reproducibility of results by yielding less or almost no variation in the effect sizes for Lab-Mue.
source: Yet again, the formation of model ensembles increased the reproducibility of results by yielding less or almost no variation in the effect sizes (Figure 5E - Lab-Mue).
evidence: This is a finding from the Lab-Mue analysis, supported by a figure.

claim: The manual expert analysis of the Lab-Inns1 dataset revealed a significantly higher number of cFOS-positive nuclei in the basolateral amygdala (BLA) after extinction of a previously learned fear.
source: The manual expert analysis of the Lab-Inns1 dataset revealed a significantly higher number of cFOS-positive nuclei in the basolateral amygdala (BLA) after extinction of a previously learned fear, which was also reliably detected by all consensus ensembles, regardless of initiation variant (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the Lab-Inns1 analysis, supported by a figure and table.

claim: The manual expert analysis and all DL-based approaches adapted to the Lab-Inns2 dataset show increased numbers of cFOS-positive cells in the infralimbic cortex of L-DOPA/MS-275 responders compared to control mice.
source: For Lab-Inns2, the manual expert analysis as well as all DL-based approaches that were adapted to the Lab-Inns2 dataset show increased numbers of cFOS-positive cells in the infralimbic cortex of L-DOPA/MS-275 responders (Resp) compared to control (Sal) mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the Lab-Inns2 analysis, supported by a figure and table.

claim: In L-DOPA/MS-275 non-responders, no significant increase of cFOS-positive nuclei was observed.
source: However, in L-DOPA/MS-275 non-responders (nResp), we did not observe a significant increase of cFOS-positive nuclei (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the Lab-Inns2 analysis, supported by a figure and table.

claim: Manual expert analysis of the Lab-Wue2 dataset revealed a significantly lower amount of GABA-positive somata in gad1b knock-down zebrafish, compared to wildtypes.
source: Manual expert analysis of the fourth external dataset revealed a significantly lower amount of GABA-positive somata in gad1b knock-down zebrafish, compared to wildtypes (Figure 5E - Lab-Wue2, Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the Lab-Wue2 analysis, supported by a figure and table.

claim: The formation of model ensembles reduced the variation per effect in both from scratch and fine-tuned variants.
source: Consistent with the higher reliability of from scratch and fine-tuned ensemble annotations (Figure 5—figure supplement 5), this analysis shows that the formation of model ensembles reduced the variation per effect in both variants, compared to the respective individual models (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from the variation analysis across external datasets, supported by figures.

claim: The consensus ensemble workflow is reproducible for different datasets and laboratories and increases objectivity, reliability, and validity of DL-based bioimage analyses.
source: Ultimately, we conclude that our proposed ensemble consensus workflow is reproducible for different datasets and laboratories and increases objectivity, reliability, and validity of DL-based bioimage analyses.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on the comprehensive analysis of multiple datasets.

claim: DL models can hold advantages over conventional algorithms.
source: DL models can hold advantages over conventional algorithms (Caicedo et al., 2019) and have the potential to be commonly used for bioimage analysis tasks throughout the life sciences.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Caicedo et al., 2019.

claim: The performance of new bioimage analysis tools or methods is usually assessed by means of similarity measures to a certain ground truth.
source: Usually, the performance of new bioimage analysis tools or methods is assessed by means of similarity measures to a certain ground truth (Ronneberger et al., 2015; McQuin et al., 2018; Haberl et al., 2018; Falk et al., 2019; Caicedo et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations describing standard evaluation practices.

claim: The vast amount of parameters and flexibility to adapt DL models to virtually any task renders them prone to internalize unintended, but subjective human biases.
source: However, this is rarely sufficient to establish trust in the use of DL models for bioimage analysis, as the vast amount of parameters and flexibility to adapt DL models to virtually any task renders them prone to internalize unintended, but subjective human biases (von Chamier et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to von Chamier et al., 2019.

claim: Training of DL models solely on the input of a single human expert imposes a high risk of incorporating an individual human bias into the trained models.
source: In accordance with previous studies, similarity analyses revealed a substantial level of inter-rater variability in the heuristic annotations of the single experts (Schmitz et al., 1999; Collier et al., 2003; Niedworok et al., 2016). Furthermore, we confirmed the concerns already put forward by others (Falk et al., 2019; von Chamier et al., 2019) that training of DL models solely on the input of a single human expert imposes a high risk of incorporating an individual human bias into the trained models.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by data from the study and citations to previous work.

claim: Models trained on single expert annotations resemble an automation of manual image annotation, but cannot remove subjective biases from bioimage analyses.
source: We therefore conclude that models trained on single expert annotations resemble an automation of manual image annotation, but cannot remove subjective biases from bioimage analyses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of expert models.

claim: Annotations of multiple experts are imperative for two reasons: first, they mitigate or even eliminate the bias of expert-specific annotations and, second, are essential for the assessment of the model performance.
source: Importantly, only consensus ensembles led to a coincident significant increase also in the reliability and validity of fluorescent feature annotations. Our analyses also show that annotations of multiple experts are imperative for two reasons: first, they mitigate or even eliminate the bias of expert-specific annotations and, second, are essential for the assessment of the model performance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comprehensive analysis.

claim: Model-to-model variability is the main factor impairing the reproducibility of DL-based bioimage analyses.
source: Our bioimage dataset from Lab-Wue1 enabled us to look at the impact of different DL-based strategies on the results of bioimage analyses. This revealed a striking model-to-model variability as the main factor impairing the reproducibility of DL-based bioimage analyses.
evidence: This is a finding from the bioimage analysis of Lab-Wue1.

claim: Bioimage analysis performed with a consensus ensemble significantly reduces the risk of obtaining irreproducible results.
source: Thus, our data indicates that bioimage analysis performed with a consensus ensemble significantly reduces the risk of obtaining irreproducible results.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the bioimage analysis results.

claim: The adaptation of models from pretrained weights to new, yet similar data requires less training iterations, compared to the training of models from scratch.
source: In line with previous studies on transfer learning, we demonstrate that the adaptation of models from pretrained weights to new, yet similar data requires less training iterations, compared to the training of models from scratch (Falk et al., 2019).
evidence: This finding is supported by data from the external dataset analysis and a citation to Falk et al., 2019.

claim: The reliability of fine-tuned ensembles was at least equivalent to from scratch ensembles, if not higher.
source: We extend these analyses and show that the reliability of fine-tuned ensembles was at least equivalent to from scratch ensembles, if not higher.
evidence: This is a finding from the external dataset analysis.

claim: Pretrained ensembles can be used even without any adaptation, if task similarity is sufficiently high.
source: Furthermore, we also provide initial evidence that pretrained ensembles can be used even without any adaptation, if task similarity is sufficiently high.
evidence: This is a finding from the frozen model analysis.

claim: Sharing model weights from validated models in open-source libraries offers a great opportunity to provide annotation experience across labs in an open science community.
source: Sharing model weights from validated models in open-source libraries, similarly to TensorFlow Hub (https://www.tensorflow.org/hub) or PyTorch Hub (https://pytorch.org/hub/), offers a great opportunity to provide annotation experience across labs in an open science community.
evidence: This is a discussion point about the potential benefits of sharing models.

claim: The learned feature representations of cFOS consensus ensembles may serve as a good initialization for models that aim at performing nucleosomatic fluorescent label segmentation in brain slices.
source: Similarly to the pretrained and shared models of Falk et al., 2019, we surmise that the learned feature representations (i.e. model weights) of our cFOS consensus ensembles may serve as a good initialization for models that aim at performing nucleosomatic fluorescent label segmentation in brain slices.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential applications, supported by a citation to Falk et al., 2019.

claim: A model adapted to a specific data set usually outperforms a general model trained on different datasets from different domains.
